target: AG1’s claim that renewable alternative energy can scale in practice to replace fossil-fuel electricity and, more broadly, fossil fuels
objection: In the U.S., alternative energy use has never exceeded 20% historically, which AG2 uses to argue that alternatives have not demonstrated the practical ability to meet most energy demand in a large country.

target: AG1’s assumption that electricity-scale success is enough to replace fossil fuels across the whole energy system
objection: Fossil fuels are used for more than electricity; they also provide dispatchable, reliable, energy-dense supply across many energy services, so alternatives face additional barriers to replacing them beyond power generation.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can replace fossil fuels without any bridge fuel
objection: Natural gas is presented as a necessary bridge fuel because existing infrastructure and system flexibility let it reduce emissions quickly while alternatives scale up.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear is a useful part of the solution
objection: Nuclear is said to be too dangerous and ineffective to be a serious solution to global warming, because accidents such as Fukushima can wipe out its carbon-free electricity gains.

target: AG1’s claim that low U.S. alternative-energy penetration is not evidence against feasibility
objection: AG2 argues that the low historical U.S. penetration is evidence that alternatives have not yet achieved the market penetration needed to supply most energy demand.

target: AG1’s claim that wind, solar, storage, transmission, forecasting, and demand response can provide reliable dispatchable electricity at scale
objection: AG2 argues that wind and solar are variable, and that without substantial firm capacity and/or massive storage they cannot fully meet dispatchability and reliability needs of an entire national energy system.

target: AG1’s assumption that grid flexibility can be expanded fast enough to make renewables reliable at large scale
objection: AG2 says renewable variability includes multi-day and seasonal periods of low output, while forecasting, transmission, storage, and demand response have physical limits—especially for long-duration backup—so these tools cannot be expanded fast enough for a rapid fossil-fuel phase-out.

target: AG1’s claim that firm low-carbon alternatives can cover reliability needs and remove the need for fossil fuels
objection: AG2 argues that the target’s approach still requires large-scale firm low-carbon capacity, but the available firm options are mainly nuclear, hydropower, and geothermal, and those cannot be scaled fast enough to replace fossil fuels on a realistic timeline.

target: AG1’s claim that renewable-derived fuels and electrification can replace non-electric fossil-fuel uses
objection: AG2 argues that replacing transport fuels, industrial heat, and feedstocks requires major conversion-and-storage infrastructure for renewable-derived carriers, and that this infrastructure is capital-intensive, slow to deploy, and therefore creates a structural bottleneck that prevents full replacement on the needed timeline.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can supply the firm low-carbon electricity needed to scale renewable-derived fuels
objection: AG2 says nuclear is too dangerous and ineffective to be relied on as a scalable firm low-carbon source, and that accidents like Fukushima can destroy its carbon-free electricity gains.

target: AG1’s assumption that nuclear can reliably provide high-utilization electricity for renewable-fuel buildout
objection: AG2 argues that nuclear accidents and safety-driven shutdowns can eliminate nuclear’s carbon-free output for long periods, so it cannot be presumed to provide uninterrupted firm electricity throughout the buildout period.

target: AG1’s assumption that no major unforeseen physical or regulatory constraint will prevent high-reliability nuclear operation during the scaling period
objection: AG2 cites Fukushima as evidence that severe accidents and regulatory interventions can force prolonged shutdowns, undermining the assumption that nuclear reliability can simply be taken for granted during the transition.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can be counted on to provide sufficiently steady electricity for renewable-fuel production
objection: AG2 argues that nuclear cannot be turned from planned capacity into available power instantly, because new plants have long lead times and existing plants have outages, so nuclear cannot reliably deliver the rapid, continuously high throughput needed for renewable-fuel scaling.

target: AG1’s broader claim that alternative energies plus nuclear can replace fossil fuels without a bridge fuel
objection: AG2 maintains that if renewable-fuel scaling depends on uninterrupted nuclear-backed firm power, then nuclear accidents and outages make that pathway unreliable, so natural gas remains necessary as a bridge while low-carbon carrier infrastructure is built.

target: AG1’s claim that high historical renewable penetration and existing know-how show the transition is feasible
objection: AG2 argues that the U.S. has never exceeded about 20% alternative energy historically, which indicates a systemic deployment or integration constraint on how quickly alternatives can grow in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that low-carbon generation and conversion/storage infrastructure can be scaled fast enough for full decarbonization
objection: AG2 says the combined need to scale both low-carbon generation and the conversion/storage infrastructure creates a major practical bottleneck that prevents timely expansion to the levels needed for rapid renewable-fuel buildouts.
